Power Calculation for Exact Agreement/Tolerance Test

Source: R/power_exact_agreement.R
power_agreement_exact.Rd

Computes sample size, power, or other parameters for the exact method of assessing agreement between two measurement methods, as described in Shieh (2019). This method tests whether the central portion of paired differences falls within specified bounds.

Usage

power_agreement_exact(
  n = NULL,
  delta = NULL,
  mu = 0,
  sigma = NULL,
  p0_star = 0.95,
  power = NULL,
  alpha = 0.05,
  max_iter = 1000,
  m = 1,
  icc = 0
)

Arguments

n

Number of subject pairs (sample size), or the number of subjects when m > 1

delta

Maximum allowable difference bound (half-width of tolerance interval)

mu

Mean of paired differences

sigma

Standard deviation of paired differences. With clustered data (m > 1), the total SD of the differences.

p0_star

The coverage proportion (content) of the tolerance interval. Central proportion under null hypothesis (default = 0.95)

power

Target power (probability of rejecting false null)

alpha

Significance level (Type I error rate, default = 0.05, Confidence level = 1-alpha)

max_iter

Maximum iterations for gamma computation (default = 1000)

m

number of paired measurements per subject (default 1, independent pairs). See the "Clustered data" section.

icc

intraclass correlation of the paired differences (between-subject share of the variance of the differences), in [0, 1). Ignored when m = 1. This is not the test-retest ICC of the measurements themselves.

Value

An object of class "power.htest", a list with components:

n

Sample size (pairs, or subjects when m > 1)

delta

Maximum allowable difference bound

mu

Mean of differences

sigma

Standard deviation of differences

p0_star

Central proportion (null hypothesis)

p1_star

Central proportion (alternative hypothesis)

alpha

Significance level

power

Power of the test

critical_value

Critical value for test statistic

m, icc

The clustering inputs

n.obs

Total number of pairs, n * m

method

Description of the method

note

Additional notes

Details

This function implements the exact agreement test procedure of Shieh (2019) for method comparison studies. The test evaluates whether the central proportion of the distribution of paired differences lies within the interval [-delta, delta].

The null hypothesis is: H0: theta_(1-p) <= -delta or delta <= theta_p The alternative is: H1: -delta < theta_(1-p) and theta_p < delta

where p = (1 + p0_star)/2, and theta_p represents the 100p-th percentile of the paired differences.

Specify three of: n, delta, power, and sigma. The fourth will be calculated. If mu is not specified, it defaults to 0. A sample size can only be found when the proportion of differences within [-delta, delta] under the alternative (p1_star) exceeds p0_star; otherwise power cannot exceed alpha and an error is returned.

Tolerance Interval Interpretation:

The parameter p0_star represents the tolerance coverage proportion, i.e., the proportion of the population that must fall within the specified bounds [-delta, delta] under the null hypothesis. This is conceptually related to tolerance intervals, but formulated as a hypothesis test rather than an estimation problem.

The power is that of Shieh's test (reject H0 when xbar -/+ gamma \* SE lies within [-delta, delta]; for independent pairs this test is reported by agree_test()). It is not the probability that tolerance limits from tolerance_limit() fall within [-delta, delta]; that decision rule is less powerful. In simulations at a planned power of 0.80, it was about 0.66 for independent pairs and about 0.57 to 0.61 for clustered data (m = 3, icc = 0.1 to 0.6). Allow a larger sample if the analysis will be based on tolerance limits.

Note: This differs from Bland-Altman's "95% limits of agreement," which are confidence intervals for the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, not tolerance intervals.

Clustered test statistic

With m > 1, the test is Shieh's test with the standard error of the mean difference taken as S \* sqrt(DEFF / (n \* m)), i.e. with the design effect treated as known. No function in this package currently carries out that clustered test, so treat the clustered power as a planning approximation.

Clustered data

When each of n subjects contributes m paired measurements (repeated measures, or several pairs per subject), the pairs are not independent and treating n * m pairs as independent overstates precision. Setting m and icc accounts for this under a balanced one-way random-effects (compound symmetry) model for the differences:

  • The mean difference has variance sigma^2 \* DEFF / (n \* m), with design effect DEFF = 1 + (m - 1) \* icc, so the effective sample size for the mean is n \* m / DEFF.

  • The total variance is estimated as S^2 = MSB / m + (m - 1) / m \* MSW, whose distribution is a weighted sum of two independent chi-square variables with n - 1 and n(m - 1) degrees of freedom. This distribution is integrated numerically in place of the single chi-square of the independent case. It is more skewed than a Satterthwaite approximation suggests, which matters when icc is large.

Under these assumptions the calculation is exact (it agrees with simulation to Monte Carlo error), and m = 1 gives exactly the published method. The simple design effect 1 + (m - 1) \* icc applied to the whole sample size overstates the penalty, because the SD has a much smaller design effect, 1 + (m - 1) \* icc^2. Unbalanced designs, other correlation structures, or several levels of nesting are not covered; use simulation for those.

icc is the ICC of the differences, which can be estimated from pilot data with an intercept-only mixed model on the differences (e.g. lme4::lmer(diff ~ 1 + (1 | id))), and sigma is then the square root of the sum of the two variance components.

References

Shieh, G. (2019). Assessing Agreement Between Two Methods of Quantitative Measurements: Exact Test Procedure and Sample Size Calculation. Statistics in Biopharmaceutical Research, 12(3), 352-359. doi:10.1080/19466315.2019.1677495

Bland, J.M. and Altman, D.G. (2007). Agreement between methods of measurement with multiple observations per individual. Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics, 17(4), 571-582. doi:10.1080/10543400701329422

Examples

# Example 1: Find required sample size
power_agreement_exact(delta = 7, mu = 0.5, sigma = 2.5,
                      p0_star = 0.95, power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#>      Power for Exact Method for Assessing Agreement Between Two Methods 
#> 
#>               n = 34
#>           delta = 7
#>              mu = 0.5
#>           sigma = 2.5
#>         p0_star = 0.95
#>         p1_star = 0.9939889
#>           alpha = 0.05
#>           power = 0.8018401
#>  critical_value = 13.57038
#>               m = 1
#>             icc = 0
#>           n.obs = 34
#> 
#> NOTE: H0: Central 95% of differences not within [-delta, delta]
#>      H1: Central 99.4% of differences within [-delta, delta] 
#>      n is the number of pairs. Two measurements per unit; one for each method.
#> 

# Example 2: Calculate power for given sample size
power_agreement_exact(n = 15, delta = 0.1, mu = 0.011,
                      sigma = 0.044, p0_star = 0.80, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#>      Power for Exact Method for Assessing Agreement Between Two Methods 
#> 
#>               n = 15
#>           delta = 0.1
#>              mu = 0.011
#>           sigma = 0.044
#>         p0_star = 0.8
#>         p1_star = 0.9726269
#>           alpha = 0.05
#>           power = 0.8315343
#>  critical_value = 6.391127
#>               m = 1
#>             icc = 0
#>           n.obs = 15
#> 
#> NOTE: H0: Central 80% of differences not within [-delta, delta]
#>      H1: Central 97.3% of differences within [-delta, delta] 
#>      n is the number of pairs. Two measurements per unit; one for each method.
#> 

# Example 3: Find required delta for given power and sample size
power_agreement_exact(n = 50, mu = 0, sigma = 2.5,
                      p0_star = 0.95, power = 0.90, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#>      Power for Exact Method for Assessing Agreement Between Two Methods 
#> 
#>               n = 50
#>           delta = 6.656157
#>              mu = 0
#>           sigma = 2.5
#>         p0_star = 0.95
#>         p1_star = 0.9922429
#>           alpha = 0.05
#>           power = 0.9
#>  critical_value = 15.8932
#>               m = 1
#>             icc = 0
#>           n.obs = 50
#> 
#> NOTE: H0: Central 95% of differences not within [-delta, delta]
#>      H1: Central 99.2% of differences within [-delta, delta] 
#>      n is the number of pairs. Two measurements per unit; one for each method.
#> 

# Example 4: Clustered data, 3 pairs per subject, ICC of the differences 0.15
power_agreement_exact(delta = 7, mu = 0.5, sigma = 2.5,
                      p0_star = 0.95, power = 0.80, m = 3, icc = 0.15)
#> 
#>      Power for Exact Method for Assessing Agreement Between Two Methods 
#> 
#>               n = 12
#>           delta = 7
#>              mu = 0.5
#>           sigma = 2.5
#>         p0_star = 0.95
#>         p1_star = 0.9939889
#>           alpha = 0.05
#>           power = 0.8047327
#>  critical_value = 12.17416
#>               m = 3
#>             icc = 0.15
#>           n.obs = 36
#> 
#> NOTE: H0: Central 95% of differences not within [-delta, delta]
#>      H1: Central 99.4% of differences within [-delta, delta] 
#>      n is the number of subjects, each with m = 3 paired measurements (n.obs pairs in total).
#>      Assumes balanced compound symmetry with ICC of the differences = 0.15.
#>
